title: Non-parametric Circular Inference
notes: Open by separating this chapter from the preceding von Mises inference. Here the data analysis begins with operations that survive weak modeling assumptions: reflection signs, circular ranks, uniform scores, empirical distribution differences, runs, and grouped score resultants. The source span is pages 145 through 158 in print and 161 through 174 in the PDF.

title: The Distribution-free Route
notes: Use the route diagram as the lecture map. The chapter does not abandon geometry; it replaces density formulas with transformations of cyclic order. Each stop asks what information remains valid when the origin direction, concentration model, or exact spacing pattern is not trusted.

title: What Distribution-free Means On A Circle
notes: Stress that distribution-free does not mean structure-free. A circular procedure still has to respect rotation, wraparound, and the absence of a natural first observation. The safe objects are side, order, rank, score vector, and label sequence, because these objects can be recomputed after changing the cut point.

title: Symmetry Around A Proposed Axis
notes: Introduce the first one-sample problem by rotating the proposed axis to a convenient reference. The sign test counts which open semicircle receives each observation, while the signed-rank version attaches more weight to points farther from the axis. The point is to test balance without fitting a circular density.

title: Signed Ranks Keep Distance Information
notes: The sign count is intentionally coarse: seven observations on one side and four on the other are not enough by themselves to describe the geometry. Signed ranks add a second layer by ordering the angular distances back to the axis line, so distant imbalances contribute more than small local deviations.

title: L-fold Symmetry By Rotation Copies
notes: For l-fold symmetry, the computational move is to generate rotated copies separated by 360 over l degrees. If the expanded set is closed under the generator, a subsequent uniformity or score diagnostic can examine whether the data respect that repeated rotational pattern rather than only a single reflection axis.

title: Circular Ranks Need A Declared Cut
notes: Circular ranks are assigned after choosing a cut point, but the interpretation must not depend on pretending that the cut is a real boundary. Ties deserve explicit handling because the usual rank tests are continuous-data procedures. The deck uses tiny deterministic separation only as a transparent ranking convention.

title: Uniform Scores Replace Spacings
notes: Uniform scores are the key rank transport. After ordering the combined sample, rank r is placed at the r-th root-of-unity position, so observed arc lengths are discarded while cyclic order is retained. The complete score set sums to zero, which later explains a useful two-sample symmetry.

title: Two Samples As Score Resultants
notes: Once each observation has a uniform score, a labeled subset receives a resultant vector. If sample A and sample B are thoroughly interleaved, their resultants tend to be short. If the labels occupy different arcs, the subset resultant length grows and flags a distributional difference.

title: Empirical CDF Contrast Around The Circle
notes: The EDF view keeps more of the ordered label history than a single resultant. Walk around the circle and update the difference between the two empirical proportions. Kuiper reads the vertical range of that walk, while Watson centers the same walk and accumulates squared fluctuation.

title: Runs Read Label Clustering
notes: Runs are a deliberately simple diagnostic for separation. On a closed circle the run count is the number of label transitions, so a two-sample circular run count is even. Long arcs occupied by one label create few transitions even when the exact angular spacings are ignored.

title: Q-sample Uniform-score Test
notes: Move from two labels to q labels by computing a score resultant for each group and adding their squared lengths. The notebook example has three groups, so the large-sample reference has 2q minus 2 degrees of freedom. The statistic is suggestive but not extreme for the displayed values.

title: What Each Statistic Can See
notes: Use the comparison board to prevent a common mistake: these procedures are not interchangeable names for the same signal. Score resultants emphasize first-moment separation in rank space, EDF methods inspect the whole ordered discrepancy, runs isolate clustering, and symmetry tests ask a one-sample reflection question.

title: Invariance Lab: Rotate, Swap, Disturb Ties
notes: The notebook lab is evidence that the procedures are geometric. A simultaneous rotation preserves the score resultant, Kuiper value, Watson value, and runs count. Swapping labels reverses some vectors but keeps paired squared lengths. Reversing tied blocks exposes sensitivity that should be reported, not hidden.

title: Pitfalls In Circular Rank Tests
notes: Close the technical part with failure modes. A cut point can create a false sense of first and last observations, a tie rule can decide a marginal rank statistic, and a small sample can make asymptotic references look more precise than the data justify. The remedy is explicit reporting.

title: Operational Checklist
notes: End with a reusable workflow. State the null symmetry or equality question, rotate only as a coordinate convenience, declare the cut and tie rule, compute ranks or signs, choose the statistic for the signal type, verify rotation invariance, and interpret the result as distribution-free evidence rather than a fitted model.
